content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has a fundamental mandate to assist its Member States in achieving the highest attainable standard of health for all individuals. This includes addressing sexual and reproductive health (SRH) issues, which were further clarified during the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD). Since then, there has been significant progress in defining human rights standards related to SRH and in developing rights-based approaches to health, including SRH. In 2004, the World Health Assembly adopted a reproductive health strategy aimed at accelerating progress toward international development goals. This strategy emphasized ensuring access to contraceptive information and services while promoting and protecting human rights. More recently, initiatives such as the United Nations Secretary-General’s global campaign Every Woman Every Child, launched in 2010, and the establishment of the Commission on Information and Accountability for Women’s and Children’s Health in 2011, have provided a framework for strengthening the use of human rights to improve all aspects of SRH, including access to contraceptive information and services. Contraception offers clear health benefits by preventing unintended pregnancies, which in turn reduces maternal and infant mortality and morbidity. This is particularly beneficial for adolescent girls, who face higher risks of medical complications during pregnancy and are often forced to compromise their education and employment opportunities, leading to poverty and lower educational attainment. Access to contraception also empowers individuals to take control of their sexuality, health, and reproduction, contributing to a satisfying sexual life. Human rights, as guaranteed by international and regional treaties, as well as national constitutions and laws, include the right to non-discrimination, the right to life, survival, and development, the right to the highest attainable standard of health, and the rights to education and information. These rights have been applied by authoritative human rights bodies, such as UN treaty-monitoring bodies, international and regional courts, and national courts, to a wide range of SRH issues, including access to contraceptive information and services. All rights are interdependent and indivisible. For example, the right to health, which includes access to health services and health-related information, cannot be fulfilled without promoting and protecting the rights to education and information, as individuals must be aware of health services to use them effectively. All states have ratified at least one human rights treaty, and 80% have ratified at least four. When governments ratify international human rights treaties, they are legally obligated to ensure that their national laws, policies, and practices align with their international obligations. Governments achieve this by respecting, protecting, and fulfilling rights. Respecting rights involves refraining from interfering with the enjoyment of rights, such as not criminalizing methods of preventing unwanted pregnancies. Protecting rights requires enacting laws to prevent violations of rights by state authorities or non-state actors and ensuring mechanisms for redress, such as guarantees against forced sterilization. Fulfilling rights involves taking active steps to establish institutions and procedures that enable individuals to enjoy their guaranteed rights, such as providing appropriate training for healthcare providers, fostering public participation in the design and monitoring of services, and ensuring equitable geographic access to services. Among the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) agreed upon in 2001, Target 5b called for universal access to reproductive health by 2015, with one indicator being the extent to which the need for contraception has been met. However, evidence shows that in many countries, laws, policies, and practices are not always consistent with human rights obligations, creating barriers to achieving the MDGs and the highest attainable standard of SRH. Some state actors limit the availability of certain contraceptive methods, such as emergency contraception, or fail to ensure regular stocks and affordable distribution of contraceptives nationwide. Additionally, insufficient investment in quality family planning and contraceptive services, including trained staff and a full range of methods accessible to the entire population, remains a challenge. States have an obligation to review and revise any related laws, policies, and practices to ensure they support all human rights obligations and development goals related to SRH. Systematic integration of human rights into law, policy, and program development is essential to facilitate the timely provision of quality services. This requires addressing underlying determinants of health, such as gender inequality, and establishing participatory, transparent, and responsive processes. Evidence demonstrates that respecting, protecting, and fulfilling human rights contributes to positive sexual health outcomes. For instance, introducing sexuality education promotes healthy adolescent development and responsible sexual and reproductive health behaviors, leading to outcomes such as delayed sexual debut, reduced unintended pregnancies, and lower levels of sexual risk-taking. Providing contraceptive information and services that respect individual privacy, confidentiality, and informed choice, along with a wide range of safe contraceptive methods, increases satisfaction and continued use of contraception. Health policies and programs are more effective when affected populations participate in their development. The legal environment plays a critical role in sexual health when aligned with human rights standards. For example, eliminating third-party authorization requirements for women respects their rights to autonomy and privacy and increases access to SRH services. Similarly, liberalizing abortion laws reduces unsafe abortions, leading to decreased maternal mortality and morbidity. Grounding contraceptive policies and programs in a human rights framework improves access to information and services, ensures active participation of individuals in decision-making processes, and calls for the removal of policy or programmatic barriers while establishing clear accountability mechanisms. To address the urgent need for contraception, reduce inequities in access to information and services, and ensure that human rights are not infringed, this guidance focuses on recommendations related to promoting and protecting human rights in the provision of contraceptive information and services. It recognizes that contraception is only one part of the broader spectrum of SRH information and services to which all individuals are entitled. It also acknowledges that no contraceptive method is 100% effective in preventing pregnancy and that other factors, such as coercive sexual relations and socioeconomic or political circumstances, may prevent women from using contraception. Therefore, contraception alone cannot entirely eliminate the need for access to safe abortion services. This document aims to provide guidance on actions to ensure that the various human rights dimensions discussed above are systematically and clearly integrated into the provision of contraceptive information and services. It is intended for use by policymakers, managers, and other stakeholders in the health sector at the programmatic, national, and international levels. While this guidance provides broad recommendations, it will require further elaboration and adaptation to specific country contexts. It is not exhaustive and serves as a first step to address human rights obligations related to the provision of contraceptive information and services. It will be regularly expanded and updated.
